newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Robotics faster modem gives it edge - analysts.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Robotics faster modem gives it edge - analysts.

text.p: Modem giant U.S. Robotics Corp, having announced Wednesday its long-awaited faster modem will be available in early 1997, will have the advantage of a quick entrance to the market and simple upgrades, analysts said.
"It would be at least a six-month market lead, a six-month window of opportunity," said Rakesh Sood, an analyst for Hambrecht & Quist.
U.S. Robotics said it has developed a modem and a central hub used by online service providers with which Internet surfers can download data at speeds of 56 kilobits per second.
The fastest modem currently on the market is 33.6 kbps.

The company said it will begin field testing of the "x2" technology in November and expects to make available software to upgrade both the modems and the hubs currently on the market in January 1997. In February, the actual products will be available, U.S. Robotics said.

"We think they have a unique strategic advantage with this because they are first to market and have compelling technology," said Eric Blachno, an analyst for Bear Sterns who initiated coverage of U.S. Robotics on Wednesday with a buy rating. "The demand is going to be huge."

On Wednesday Lucent Technologies Inc said it would be shipping its first processing chip based on the 56 kbps technology by the end of the first quarter. Motorola Inc has also said it plans to introduce the new technology in 1997 and Rockwell International Corp's semiconductor unit has said it plans to demonstrate 56 kilobit technology in November.

Analysts said, however, that U.S. Robotics' ability to upgrade using software instead of equipment changes is key for a number of reasons and will help reaffirm the company's dominant market share in both the personal modem and central hub markets.

First, a switch to the faster hubs and modems is quick and relatively cheap with software compared to a complete change in hardware. Analysts said the upgrade for online services can be made overnight.

"It (equipment changes) usually delays deployment of new technological capabilities," Blachno said. "Given the pace of the race to deploy this technology, we believe the software upgradability will serve as a substantial advantage."

Second, U.S. Robotics said it will charge a "nominal" fee for upgrades -- that will mean clients will not put off buying new modems in anticipation of faster transmission speeds, and the small upgrade fee will just help margins.
"Software sales obviously have a larger gross margin than hardware," said Eric Buck, an analyst for Donaldson Lufkin and Jenrette.
And although most analysts see U.S. Robotics leading the way to set the industry standard, even small modifications are simple, they said.
"With the unique software-based architecture, you will be able to upgrade to whatever standards are determined," Buck said.

And as analysts had expected, U.S. Robotics already has set up partners. America Online, CompuServe, IBM Global Network and Netcom have all said they will run field tests on the x2 technology in November.

"They have taken advantage of these capabilities and the proof is their terrific market share gains," Blachno said. "We believe they are likely to continue gaining share because of the flexibility of the products."
